clusters.title: International Court of Justice Rules Myanmar Committed Genocide Against Rohingya
clusters.summary: The International Court of Justice (ICJ) has ruled that Myanmar is guilty of genocide against the Rohingya minority, marking a historic decision as it is the first time a state has been held accountable for genocide by the court. The ruling, passed by a narrow margin of nine votes to six, pertains to the military crackdown in 2017 that resulted in thousands of deaths and widespread displacement of the Rohingya people. The court has called for reparations and the safe return of refugees.

explore_lenses.label: How did this case reach a final judgment?
explore_lenses.title: A seven-year legal process tested competing accounts
explore_lenses.summary: The ruling followed a case filed by The Gambia in 2019 over the 2016-17 operations in northern Rakhine, with merits hearings held in January 2026. Myanmar characterized the operations as counter-terrorism; the Court ultimately found that genocide had been committed.

claims.text: The Gambia instituted the case in November 2019, and the ICJ heard merits arguments from 12 to 29 January 2026, including witness and expert testimony.

Myanmar's counsel argued that the operations responded to attacks by the Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army, were counter-terrorism measures rather than genocide, and that key evidence was insufficient or unreliable.
The Court's record included Rohingya and former-military-defector testimony, UN and IIMM material, satellite evidence, NGO reports, and Myanmar military documents and operational reports.

explore_lenses.label: What must Myanmar do next?
explore_lenses.title: Reparations and a two-year reporting deadline
explore_lenses.summary: The judgment orders measures aimed at accountability, non-repetition and repair, while leaving the amount and modalities of compensation for a later phase. It is final and binding, but implementation will depend on Myanmar's compliance and international follow-through.

claims.text: Myanmar must investigate suspected perpetrators, prosecute and punish them where warranted, provide guarantees of non-repetition, and adopt restitution measures including safe, voluntary and dignified return, family reunification, property return and rehabilitation.

Myanmar must compensate the Rohingya for damage not remedied through restitution; the Court retained the question of the compensation amount and modalities and required Myanmar to submit a restitution-and-compensation report within two years.

UN Secretary-General António Guterres said Myanmar must comply with the judgment and called on the international community to strengthen collective action and support an inclusive political solution addressing the crisis's root causes.
Whether the orders produce prompt change is uncertain: the ICJ's judgment is legally binding, but the Court does not directly enforce compliance.

event_overview.subject: US House Leadership
event_overview.summary: This event concerns House Democrats’ selection of Hakeem Jeffries as their nominee for Speaker for the 120th Congress, following the 2026 elections. facts.label: Constitutional basis
facts.value: Article I, Section 2 of the U.S. Constitution provides that the House of Representatives chooses its Speaker and other officers.

facts.label: How the Speaker is chosen
facts.value: The Speaker is elected by the entire House, while each party’s Members select their own leadership and typically put forward a Speaker candidate through party caucus processes.

facts.label: Role of the office
facts.value: The Speaker serves as the House’s presiding officer and administrative head and is ordinarily the leader of the chamber’s majority party.

facts.label: Nominee
facts.value: Jeffries is a Democratic representative from New York who has served as House Democratic Leader during the 118th and 119th Congresses; House historical records list his House service beginning in January 2013.

facts.label: 2026 party action
facts.value: A November 18, 2026 House Democratic caucus-related announcement described Jeffries as the party’s nominee, or “Speaker Designate,” for the next Congress; the designation remains distinct from a House-wide Speaker election.

claims.text: A new Congress begins at noon on January 3 of each odd-numbered year unless Congress sets another date by law; the House has been described by a member’s official release as formally electing the Speaker on January 3, 2027.

With Democrats expected to take control of the chamber in January, the nomination puts Jeffries on track to seek the speakership and, if elected by the full House, become its first Black speaker. sections.heading: House Speaker Election Process
sections.body: The Democratic Caucus nomination is separate from the formal election of a speaker. Party caucuses generally select their candidates privately, but representatives-elect choose the speaker on the House floor. The new Congress is scheduled to begin at noon on Jan. 3, 2027, and the House has been described as formally electing its speaker that day. A candidate must win a numerical majority of votes cast for a named person; members voting “present” do not count toward that total.

In his Nov. 4 candidacy letter, Jeffries emphasized affordability, accountability and American values, and described immigration enforcement as fair, just and humane.

event_overview.title: About Iran War
event_overview.subject: Iran War
event_overview.summary: The Iran War is an ongoing armed conflict centered on military operations by the United States and Israel against Iran, Iranian retaliation, and a parallel struggle over security and commercial navigation in the Strait of Hormuz. The conflict has also affected neighboring Gulf states, international shipping, energy markets, and diplomatic efforts to establish a ceasefire or longer-term settlement.

facts.label: Start and status
facts.value: U.S. and Israeli military operations against Iran began on February 28, 2026; major combat was paused by an April 7 U.S.-Iran ceasefire, but hostilities and attacks affecting shipping resumed in July 2026.

facts.label: Central geography
facts.value: The Strait of Hormuz is a principal focus of the conflict. It links the Persian Gulf with the Gulf of Oman, lies within Iranian and Omani territorial waters, and is a major route for oil and liquefied-natural-gas trade.

facts.label: Main participants and spillover
facts.value: The core interstate conflict involves Iran and the United States, with Israel participating alongside the United States; attacks and threats have also affected commercial vessels and Gulf countries including Bahrain, Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates.

facts.label: Diplomatic framework
facts.value: On June 17, 2026, the United States and Iran signed a memorandum of understanding that envisaged ending military operations and Iranian arrangements for safe commercial passage through the Strait for 60 days; its interpretation and implementation became contested.

facts.label: International legal and humanitarian con
facts.value: United Nations Security Council documentation has emphasized that transit passage through the Strait should not be impeded, called for protection of civilian infrastructure and commercial shipping, and urged de-escalation and diplomacy.

event_overview.scope_note: The selected Muninn timeline covers a short period of escalation and negotiation in late July 2026, especially threats, maritime-security incidents and U.S. domestic war-powers debate; it does not cover the conflict's full military, diplomatic, humanitarian or regional history.

explore_lenses.summary: The reported strike locations were not only a dense civilian urban area but included the UNESCO-protected zone of Odesa’s historic centre. claims.text: Odesa City Council said some of the November 18 strike locations were within the UNESCO-protected zone, including Yevropeiska Street.
UNESCO lists the Historic Centre of Odesa as a World Heritage property, inscribed in 2023 and retained on the List of World Heritage in Danger.

UNESCO describes the property as a densely built central area containing residential, public, cultural, commercial and administrative buildings, underscoring why damage there can affect both civilians and heritage fabric.

UNESCO’s 2025 monitoring assessment said the site’s conservation remained critical because of the ongoing war and intensified missile and drone attacks, while noting that Ukrainian authorities had carried out emergency interventions after prior attacks.

event_overview.title: About Iran War
event_overview.subject: Iran War
event_overview.summary: The Iran War is an ongoing armed conflict centered on military operations by the United States and Israel against Iran, Iranian retaliation, and a parallel struggle over security and commercial navigation in the Strait of Hormuz. The conflict has also affected neighboring Gulf states, international shipping, energy markets, and diplomatic efforts to establish a ceasefire or longer-term settlement.

facts.label: Start and status
facts.value: U.S. and Israeli military operations against Iran began on February 28, 2026; major combat was paused by an April 7 U.S.-Iran ceasefire, but hostilities and attacks affecting shipping resumed in July 2026.

facts.label: Central geography
facts.value: The Strait of Hormuz is a principal focus of the conflict. It links the Persian Gulf with the Gulf of Oman, lies within Iranian and Omani territorial waters, and is a major route for oil and liquefied-natural-gas trade.

facts.label: Main participants and spillover
facts.value: The core interstate conflict involves Iran and the United States, with Israel participating alongside the United States; attacks and threats have also affected commercial vessels and Gulf countries including Bahrain, Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates.

facts.label: Diplomatic framework
facts.value: On June 17, 2026, the United States and Iran signed a memorandum of understanding that envisaged ending military operations and Iranian arrangements for safe commercial passage through the Strait for 60 days; its interpretation and implementation became contested.

facts.label: International legal and humanitarian con
facts.value: United Nations Security Council documentation has emphasized that transit passage through the Strait should not be impeded, called for protection of civilian infrastructure and commercial shipping, and urged de-escalation and diplomacy.

event_overview.subject: Space Exploration
event_overview.summary: The event centers on SpaceX’s Starship Flight 15 test, which demonstrated recovery of the Starship upper stage at Starbase, Texas after an orbital mission. facts.label: Mission timing and location
facts.value: Flight 15 launched from SpaceX’s Starbase site near Boca Chica in Cameron County, Texas, on November 13, 2026; the Starship upper stage returned to the site and was caught by the launch tower on November 14. facts.label: Vehicle format
facts.value: Starship is a two-stage launch system comprising the Starship upper stage and the Super Heavy booster. SpaceX’s stated design approach is for both stages to return to Earth and be caught by mechanical arms on the launch tower for inspection, refurbishment, and reuse.

facts.label: Test outcome
facts.value: The upper stage completed an orbital flight and was recovered at the launch tower, while the Super Heavy booster diverted to a water landing rather than completing its planned tower catch.

facts.label: Regulatory setting
facts.value: Commercial Starship/Super Heavy launches from Boca Chica are regulated by the Federal Aviation Administration’s Office of Commercial Space Transportation. FAA licensing reviews address public safety, national-security and foreign-policy concerns, insurance, and environmental effects.

explore_lenses.title: Engineering trade-offs extended the mission
explore_lenses.summary: Voyager’s distance reflects its 1977 launch trajectory and decades of operational conservation. Mission engineers have repeatedly traded science capability for electrical power and spacecraft health.

claims.text: Voyager 1 launched on September 5, 1977, completed close flybys of Jupiter and Saturn, and then continued outward on an interstellar trajectory.
Its radioisotope power source loses about 4 watts of electrical power each year, forcing the team to switch off heaters, systems, and science instruments over time.

Kareem Badaruddin, Voyager mission manager at JPL, described the April 2026 shutdown of Voyager 1’s low-energy charged-particle instrument as the best available option for preserving the spacecraft, despite the loss of that science capability.
As of NASA’s April 2026 instrument-status update, Voyager 1 retained only its magnetometer and plasma-wave subsystem as active science instruments; its cameras have been off since 1990.

sections.heading: Voyager 1’s Interstellar Journey
sections.body: Launched on Sept. 5, 1977, Voyager 1 made close flybys of Jupiter and Saturn before continuing on an interstellar trajectory. It entered interstellar space in 2012 and is one of only two spacecraft still operating beyond the heliosphere, the Sun’s protective bubble of particles and magnetic fields. Its remaining observations provide direct local measurements of magnetic fields and plasma waves in interstellar space, rather than relying only on remote observations.

sections.heading: Voyager 1 Faces Power Limits
sections.body: The light-day distance is not a new physical boundary in space; its practical scientific value depends on the continuity and quality of Voyager 1’s remaining measurements. Its radioisotope power source loses about 4 watts of electrical power annually, requiring NASA to shut down heaters, systems and instruments over time. After the low-energy charged-particle instrument was turned off in April 2026, the magnetometer and plasma-wave subsystem remained Voyager 1’s only active science instruments; its cameras have been off since 1990.

sections.heading: NASA Maintains Voyager 1 Operations
sections.body: NASA says recent power-saving changes should keep the current science-instrument suite operating at least through the spacecrafts’ 50th launch anniversaries in summer 2027. Project manager Suzanne Dodd said the team listens to Voyager 1 daily and sends commands weekly. At its current distance, a command takes about 24 hours to arrive and a response requires another 24 hours to return.

unresolved.text: NASA had not publicly identified the cause of Voyager 1’s missing science and engineering telemetry in its Nov. 19 update, or provided a timetable for restoring it.
Aging hardware creates risks beyond the spacecraft’s planned power decline, leaving the lifetime of individual instruments and communications systems uncertain.
